nameStory: Corn cockle gets its name from its habit of growing as a weed in grain fields, particularly corn and wheat crops. The 'cockle' part comes from an old word meaning 'weed' or 'tares' - those unwanted plants that farmers would find mixed in with their precious grain. Its scientific name Agrostemma literally means 'field garland' in Greek, referring to how its pretty pink flowers would crown the crop fields like a decorative wreath.
description: Corn cockle is a tall, slender annual wildflower that can reach 2-4 feet in height. It has a graceful, upright growth habit with narrow, silvery-green leaves and striking magenta-pink flowers that bloom at the tips of long stems. The whole plant has a soft, fuzzy texture and an old-fashioned cottage garden appearance. Originally from Europe, it's now quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special treat for wildflower enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five bright magenta-pink petals that feel papery to the touch, with distinctive dark veining running through each petal. The flowers are about 1-2 inches across and sit atop long, slender stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They have a silvery-green color and no teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and elegantly upright, growing 2-4 feet high with a branching pattern that creates an open, airy appearance. The plant sways gracefully in the breeze.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, round black seeds that rattle inside papery capsules when mature. The seeds have a rough, bumpy texture and are quite poisonous.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy but slender stems covered in fine, soft hairs that give them a downy feel. The stems are pale green and branch near the top to hold multiple flowers.

habitat: Corn cockle prefers disturbed soils and open areas, particularly old agricultural fields, roadsides, and waste places. In New England, you're most likely to find it in areas that were once farmed or in sandy, well-drained soils. It thrives in full sun and doesn't compete well with established vegetation, so look for it in recently disturbed ground or sparse grasslands.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as fuzzy, silvery-green rosettes close to the ground. The distinctive opposite leaves and soft, hairy texture are already apparent on seedlings.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, with showy magenta-pink flowers opening from June through August. This is when the plant is most easily identified and at its most spectacular.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, eventually turning brown and papery. The black seeds inside rattle when shaken, and the whole plant begins to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring. No above-ground parts persist through winter.

funFact: Corn cockle seeds are so poisonous that they were once a serious problem when accidentally harvested with grain - bread made from contaminated flour could actually kill people! The seeds contain compounds called saponins that are toxic to both humans and livestock, which is one reason farmers worked so hard to eliminate this beautiful but dangerous weed from their fields.
confusionNotes: The bright pink flowers might be confused with other members of the pink family, but corn cockle's tall, graceful stature and fuzzy, silvery leaves make it distinctive. Remember: 'Fuzzy and tall with pink flowers that enthrall' - the soft, hairy texture of the whole plant is a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, corn cockle isn't actually related to corn at all. The word 'corn' in its name refers to grain crops in general (the old European meaning), not specifically to maize. This beautiful wildflower has become increasingly rare due to modern farming practices and herbicide use, making it a conservation concern in many areas.
compareHints: Corn cockle is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local wildflowers. Compared to other pink family members like chickweeds or campions, corn cockle stands out for its much larger size, distinctive fuzzy texture, and more substantial flowers. While other pink family plants tend to be small and inconspicuous, corn cockle commands attention with its statuesque presence and showy blooms.
